clinicalPearls: Typically presents in a young adult (more often female) with subacute unilateral visual loss developing over hours to days, accompanied by pain worse on eye movement
A relative afferent pupillary defect is present, and colour vision (especially red desaturation) is impaired out of proportion to acuity
In retrobulbar neuritis the optic disc looks normal at onset ('the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing'), whereas papillitis shows a swollen disc
It is commonly the presenting or an associated feature of multiple sclerosis, so demyelination should be considered
MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast assesses the optic nerve and detects demyelinating white-matter lesions that predict multiple sclerosis risk
Vision usually recovers spontaneously over weeks; intravenous corticosteroids speed recovery but do not change final visual outcome
Atypical features (bilateral, no pain, poor recovery, severe disc swelling) should prompt consideration of neuromyelitis optica, MOG-associated disease, or an infective/compressive cause
reference.pathophysiology: Optic neuritis is inflammation and demyelination of the optic nerve, most commonly immune-mediated and associated with multiple sclerosis. An inflammatory, often T-cell-driven process attacks the myelin sheath of optic nerve axons, disrupting conduction and causing loss of visual acuity, colour vision, and contrast. Because conduction rather than the axon itself is initially affected, remyelination allows substantial recovery, though repeated or severe attacks cause axonal loss and permanent deficits with optic atrophy. Antibody-mediated variants (aquaporin-4 in neuromyelitis optica, MOG antibody disease) and infective or granulomatous causes produce similar inflammation through different mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (arteritic and non-arteritic)
Compressive optic neuropathy from tumour or aneurysm
Toxic, nutritional, or hereditary (Leber) optic neuropathy
Central retinal artery occlusion and other causes of acute visual loss
additionalInvestigations: Assessment of visual acuity, colour vision, and relative afferent pupillary defect
Visual field testing (commonly shows a central scotoma)
Contrast MRI of the brain and orbits to assess the nerve and demyelinating lesions
Aquaporin-4 and MOG antibody testing in atypical or severe cases
OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer to monitor atrophy; bloods/lumbar puncture where an infective or inflammatory cause is suspected
redFlags: Bilateral simultaneous, severe, or poorly recovering visual loss suggesting neuromyelitis optica or a non-demyelinating cause
Absence of pain or a progressive course pointing to a compressive or ischaemic optic neuropathy
Systemic features suggesting infection, sarcoidosis, or vasculitis
Older patient with headache and jaw claudication — exclude giant cell arteritis as a cause of ischaemic optic neuropathy
reference.prognosis: Most patients with typical demyelinating optic neuritis recover good vision over several weeks regardless of steroid use, though some residual colour and contrast deficits and a risk of future multiple sclerosis remain.
pitfalls: Attributing every acute optic neuropathy to demyelination and missing arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy in older patients
Assuming steroids improve the final visual outcome rather than just the speed of recovery
Overlooking neuromyelitis optica or MOG disease in atypical or severe cases that need different management
Failing to counsel on and investigate the associated risk of multiple sclerosis
management: Treat acute demyelinating attacks with high-dose intravenous corticosteroid (methylprednisolone) to accelerate visual recovery, avoiding low-dose oral corticosteroid monotherapy which raises the recurrence rate
Reserve plasma exchange for severe, steroid-refractory attacks, particularly in aquaporin-4 or MOG antibody-associated disease
In antibody-mediated relapsing disease (neuromyelitis optica spectrum), use long-term immunosuppression such as rituximab, eculizumab or mycophenolate to prevent relapses
Where MRI shows demyelinating white-matter lesions predicting multiple sclerosis, refer for neurologist-led disease-modifying therapy
Monitor visual acuity, colour vision and the retinal nerve fibre layer on OCT to track recovery and detect optic atrophy
Provide neurology and neuro-ophthalmology follow-up with contrast MRI surveillance for conversion to multiple sclerosis
Give supportive symptomatic care and reassurance regarding the usual spontaneous recovery over weeks
